title: Trump lashes out over FAA ground stop criticism | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trump bristled at scrutiny over his absence from the initial response to a historic airspace meltdown, insisting Monday that he was fully involved in managing the crisis even as he rejected any responsibility for the fallout.

Trump told reporters that he had worked out of the White House throughout the four-hour ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights nationwide, while delegating the public communications job to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

The Cabinet secretaries briefed the press on Friday, with Duffy later doing a full round of appearances on the Sunday morning news shows to try to allay concerns. The two had few definitive answers at the time for what caused the failures or how exactly they planned to fix it, even as they went out of their way to heap praise on Trump for his leadership. At one point shortly after the stoppage was enacted, Mullin admitted that “I don’t want to say that this is a crisis, but it is.”

Throughout it all, Trump remained silent on the matter for nearly two days, instead posting roughly two dozen times on Truth Social about an array of other topics, including legislation to boost the film industry and the contentious battle over one of his construction projects.

“I didn’t think there was any reason for me to do,” Trump said Monday of his lack of public involvement. “I thought they did a very good job, but I was in the Oval Office.”

The president later grew openly irritated at the suggestion he’d been prioritizing his pet projects over the airspace emergency, retorting that renovating the White House is necessary and only takes about 10 minutes of his day.

“I spend very little time to do it, and losers like you come out and they say, ‘Why are you focused on the White House?’” he said, gesturing toward the columns ringing the south portico and his new helipad. “Because the White House is a symbol of our country and the White House should look like that, and the stone should look like this.”

Trump’s dismissal followed three days of disruptions to air travel across the country, including thousands of flight delays as a result of the nationwide ground stop. Federal officials believe the crisis may have been spurred by a routine upgrade that went wrong and quickly metastasized into a broad-based communications failure.

But as officials raced to find the problem and fix it, Trump ostensibly had his mind on a range of far less urgent issues. On Friday afternoon, he posted a 294-word missive to Truth Social endorsing legislation to create a federal film incentive.

“Everyone feels strongly about the Motion Picture and Television Industry — and so do I, and we all want to save it,” he wrote.

Trump would follow that up with several more posts and reposts on Truth Social over the next couple days, including several photos of a Washington park and golf course that a judge had temporarily blocked him from closing.

The president finally addressed the airspace meltdown on Sunday morning, blaming the Biden administration for the crisis and urging Congress to pass additional funding for fixes.

Pressed on Monday about his role in calling for the ground stop, Trump refused to take direct accountability.

“I don’t take any responsibility,” he said. “They did a great job, Secretary Duffy, they acted incredibly.”

Trump reiterated that the blame for the disruptions should lay with prior administrations that failed to upgrade the air traffic control system, arguing that much of the nation’s equipment is outdated.

Duffy had earlier indicated plans to ask Congress for roughly $50 billion in additional funding for the upgrade work. Trump officials are expected to brief lawmakers on the ground stop and subsequent funding request this week.

Those plans are already facing pushback from Democrats, who have questioned how the administration is allocating an existing $12.5 billion for the FAA that was included in the GOP’s partisan centerpiece tax-and-spending legislation last year.

Trump on Monday again urged Congress to quickly pass more funding to fix the air traffic control systems, saying his administration wanted to “blow it up and put new in, and we can do it simultaneously with very little trouble.”

But as he prepared to embark on a multi-day trip to Asia, he offered little indication of the role that he would play in personally managing that high-stakes process.

“I’ve already informed Congress,” Trump said of the funding request. “I think the one good thing that comes out of it, I’m sure Congress now will give us the money to fix.”
